title: Squeezed from both sides
lede: Big-box stores beat RadioShack on selection and price, the carriers opened their own stores, and the internet took the parts business. Its own partners were also its competitors.

blocks.title: Four kinds of rival, and what became of each
blocks.subtitle: RadioShack’s store count is the only series here; our sources do not give comparable figures for the others, so they are shown by outcome only.

items.name: RadioShack
items.text: company stores at the 2001 peak and 4,216 in November 2014.[^6][^14] Two bankruptcies; the name survives under new owners.[^15][^26][^31]

items.name: Best Buy
items.text: Big-box selection and price on TVs, computers and appliances. Still operating (general knowledge, not from our sources).

items.name: Circuit City
items.text: The other big-box chain. Liquidated in 2009 (general knowledge, not from our sources), six years before RadioShack filed.

items.name: Carriers’ own stores
items.text: The carriers controlled plans, subsidies and commissions. In 2015 Sprint moved inside the stores General Wireless bought.[^20][^21]

items.name: Amazon and online parts sellers
items.text: Range, price and no trip to the mall. The shift online is general context; our sources do not quantify it.

blocks.source: RadioShack store counts from the 10-K store tables and the Q3 2014 10-Q[^6][^13][^14]. Outcomes for Best Buy, Circuit City and Amazon are general knowledge and are flagged as such.

blocks.body: RadioShack’s 10-Ks name competitors in general terms. The fates of Best Buy and [Circuit City](/circuit-city/) are well known but aren’t covered by the sources on this page, so we flag them.
